content: CD2, also known as cluster of differentiation 2, is a cell adhesion molecule that is expressed on the surface of T cells and natural killer (NK) cells. It has been referred to by several other names, including T-cell surface antigen T11/Leu-5, LFA-2, LFA-3 receptor, erythrocyte receptor, and rosette receptor. Function CD2 interacts with other adhesion molecules, such as lymphocyte function-associated antigen-3 (LFA-3, also known as CD58) in humans or CD48 in rodents. These molecules are expressed on the surfaces of other cells. Beyond its role in cell adhesion, CD2 also functions as a co-stimulatory molecule for T cells and NK cells, enhancing their activation and immune responses. Diagnostic Relevance CD2 serves as a specific marker for T cells and NK cells. This makes it a valuable tool in immunohistochemistry for identifying the presence of these cell types in tissue samples. Additionally, the majority of T-cell lymphomas and leukemias express CD2, which allows for its use in distinguishing these malignancies from B-cell neoplasms. Classification Structurally, CD2 belongs to the immunoglobulin superfamily. It contains two immunoglobulin-like domains in its extracellular region, which contribute to its functional properties. Interactions CD2 has been shown to interact with several other proteins, including CD2BP2, Lck, and PSTPIP1. These interactions are important for its role in immune cell signaling and function.
